text:
Recent research supports separating observed feedback from annotator interpretation. A 2024 study found that user feedback improved agreement when requests were ambiguous, while *Diverging Preferences* distinguishes underspecified tasks and subjective preferences from annotation errors. A 2025 annotation study recommends concise instructions, pilot examples, and preserving meaningful disagreement; longer instructions did not automatically improve agreement. These are adjacent findings, not a validated recommendation-error taxonomy. Sources: [user-feedback evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12994), [preference disagreement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14632), [annotation instructions](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668505/).

Suggested adaptation for twenty training users: one record per user–ranked-item–feedback instance, storing category, item ID, rank, verbatim rejection, supporting title/description spans, reason label, and evidence status. Separate unidentified item/insufficient metadata from explicit preference mismatch, exact duplication, and explicitly stated incompatibility, ownership, or current-intent mismatch. Require cited evidence for every substantive label; otherwise mark unknown/abstain. Repeated interactions do not establish ownership, similar titles do not establish duplication, and annotators cannot supply the user’s preferences. This is a proposed protocol, not a published taxonomy.

Have two annotators independently code the same records after a small pilot. Report raw agreement, nominal Krippendorff’s alpha or Cohen’s kappa, per-label counts and disagreements, and abstention rate with its denominator. Treat abstention as an explicit label; also report agreement among jointly decidable cases alongside coverage. Preserve original judgments before adjudication and distinguish unsupported inference from legitimate ambiguity. With only twenty users, report descriptive findings without claiming population-level preference traits.
